pass_a_gloss: to suffer, if he is of Nabal. The ventriloquist did not bring up Samuel—for it is impossible—nor having come up did he speak truth. Who this one is and through what power he came up, seek. David was besieging Jebus. Jebus was what is now called Jerusalem when it was under foreigners. The Jebusites, knowing David was a lover of the poor, put forward from the wall above blind and lame to insult him. But having taken Jerusalem he so refrained from treating badly those maimed in body that he even set a death law for his soldiers if anyone should attempt to kill a blind or lame person. For everyone striking a Jebusite lame or blind, he says, let him be touched with a dagger—that is, let him be killed; for even if they hated David's soul, still they obtain sparing. Therefore he is counted worthy of honor from all who say: lame and blind shall not enter the Lord's house—those who insulted David, whom he spared. Note that Nathan the son of David is born to him when he has taken and inhabited Jerusalem. This is Nathan whom blessed Luke genealogizes, while blessed Matthew genealogizes Solomon his brother. And from there—I mean from the mentioned sons of David—the one is said through one genealogy, the other through another. So that from here also it is shown that what God does not do but allows to happen he is said to have done. It is confessed then that Absalom's rising and Shimei's insult and his casting stones at David were not God's work. What I say is shown more clearly by David's saying: Let him curse, because the Lord has said to him, so that he may see my humiliation, and the Lord will repay me good things instead of his curse on this day. For it is plain that what was happening did not please God; and what did not please he would not have commanded to do. pass_b_english: …to suffer, if he belongs to Nabal. The medium did not bring Samuel up—that is impossible—nor did the apparition speak truth once "up." Who this was, and by what power he rose, inquire.

David was besieging Jebus—Jerusalem's name when it lay under foreigners. The Jebusites, knowing David loved the poor, set blind and lame on the wall to insult him. Having taken Jerusalem he so refused to mistreat the maimed that he even set a death penalty on any soldier who tried to kill a blind or lame person: "everyone who strikes a Jebusite lame or blind, let him be touched with the dagger"—that is, let him be killed. Even those who hated David's soul obtained sparing. So he is honored when people say the lame and blind shall not enter the Lord's house—those who insulted David, whom he spared.

Note that Nathan son of David is born after David takes and inhabits Jerusalem. This is the Nathan Luke genealogizes, while Matthew genealogizes Solomon his brother. From David's named sons, then, one line runs through one genealogy and one through another.

From this it is also shown that what God does not do, yet allows to happen, he is said to have done. Absalom's rising, Shimei's insult, and the stones cast at David were not God's work. David makes this clearer: "[[Let him curse, for the Lord has told him to; perhaps the Lord will look on my humiliation and repay me good for his curse today >> Bible:2 Samuel 16:11-12]]." What happened did not please God; what does not please him he would not command.

If in zeal for Israel and Judah Saul tried to wipe out the Gibeonites—with whom Joshua son of Nun and all the people had made covenants—and seven born from Saul's daughters were killed for it, why are the tribes not blamed while those who did no wrong pay the penalty? That would be unjust—unless one says a king Saul could not resist Israel and Judah or break the fathers' covenants with the Gibeonites. I would add: it was God's economy that Saul's whole line be consumed, as many as were ever suspected of claiming royal dignity and thus of rising against David and his children.

"The Gibeonites exposed them before the Lord on the mountain" means they did not bury the killed but left them under the sun. "They were exhausted, and Dan son of Joa of the giants' descendants took them" means the giant took those laid in the sun and killed them already spent by the heat.
